New antibody fights several flu strains at once, could make flu shot obsolete

First of all, influenza virus uses two enzymes to bind to its target cell in order to infect it. These two enzymes are neuraminidase and hemagglutinin, which both bind to sialic acid residues in target cells (fun fact: the subtype of each enzyme determines the strain of the virus, i.e., type A H1N1 has the 1 subtype of hemagglutinin and the 1 subtype of neuraminidase).

Oseltamivir is a drug that inhibits neuraminidase; therefore, it renders the virus incapable of infecting any cell. It is a really potent drug, effective against every type A or B strain of the influenza virus (even against the type A H1N1). This new antibody, "CT149 is found to neutralize all tested group 2 and some group 1 influenza A viruses by inhibiting low pH-induced, HA-mediated membrane fusion" (taken from the original article. How is it superior than Oseltamivir? I don't know. How will it make flu shot obsolete? I don't know.

Edit: I edited the link to the article.
It'll provide passive immunity not active immunity so it won't make flu shots obsolete but it'll surely be useful in the treatment of severe influenza

or for people who truly cannot get vaccinated. But I couldn't emphasize this enough. Passive immunity will never replace active immunity, NEVER. There is a reason why everyone gets vaccines are a mainstay of healthcare. They prevent disease from ever happening, not just treat the symptoms or shorten the course once someone is sick. It also prevents the disease in the population as a whole by reducing transmission. IMHO, taken all together, vaccines are the greatest medical invention (for lack of a better word) of all time and will likely never have that title taken or be replaced by a better therapy
